prg-stream-cipher.title: Stream Cipher Security from PRG Security
prg-stream-cipher.subtitle: A reduction proof: if a pseudorandom generator G is secure, then the stream cipher built from G is EAV-secure.
prg-stream-cipher.theorem: Let $G$ be a secure PRG with expansion factor $\ell(n)$. Construct a stream cipher $\Pi = (\mathsf{Gen}, \mathsf{Enc}, \mathsf{Dec})$ where $\mathsf{Gen}$ samples $k \xleftarrow{\$} \{0,1\}^n$ and $\mathsf{Enc}_k(m) = G(k) \oplus m$. If $G$ is a secure PRG, then $\Pi$ is EAV-secure (indistinguishable encryption of a single message).

steps.title: 1 · The Pseudorandom Generator
steps.claim: $G$ expands a short seed into a long, pseudorandom string.
narration: A pseudorandom generator (PRG) is a deterministic, length-expanding function:

Security means no efficient distinguisher can tell $G(s)$ (for random seed $s$) from a truly random string $r \xleftarrow{\$} \{0,1\}^{\ell(n)}$ with better than negligible advantage. We take $G$ as our hardness assumption.
steps.diagramNote: G stretches a short seed into a long output that looks random.

steps.title: 2 · Build the Stream Cipher
steps.claim: The cipher encrypts by XORing the message with the PRG output.
narration: From $G$ we build a private-key encryption scheme $\Pi$:
$\mathsf{Gen}$ picks a key $k \xleftarrow{\$} \{0,1\}^n$ (the seed). $\mathsf{Enc}_k(m) = G(k) \oplus m$. $\mathsf{Dec}_k(c) = G(k) \oplus c$.
The keystream $G(k)$ is reused never — one key, one message. Encryption is just a one-time pad whose pad is generated rather than truly random.
steps.diagramNote: Encryption = message XOR the generator output. The pad is G(k).

steps.title: 3 · The Security Goal: EAV Indistinguishability
steps.claim: No efficient A can tell which of two chosen messages was encrypted.
narration: EAV-security (indistinguishability of a single message): a challenger flips a bit $b$, A submits two equal-length messages $m_0, m_1$, receives $c = \mathsf{Enc}_k(m_b)$, and outputs a guess $b'$.
A wins when $b' = b$. $\Pi$ is EAV-secure if every efficient A wins with probability at most $\tfrac{1}{2} + \mathsf{negl}(n)$ — i.e. no better than guessing.
steps.diagramNote: A must guess which message was encrypted. Winning > 1/2 breaks the cipher.

steps.title: 4 · Assume A Breaks the Cipher
steps.claim: Assume some efficient A wins the EAV game with advantage $\varepsilon > \mathsf{negl}(n)$.
narration: For contradiction, suppose A is an efficient adversary that breaks $\Pi$: it wins the EAV game with non-negligible advantage $\varepsilon = \Pr[b'=b] - \tfrac{1}{2}$.
We will use A as a subroutine to build a distinguisher B that breaks the PRG $G$ — contradicting $G$'s security. This is the reduction.
steps.diagramNote: A wins with advantage ε. We will turn A into a PRG-distinguisher.

steps.title: 5 · The Reduction Strategy
steps.claim: Build a distinguisher B that contains A and simulates A's EAV challenger.
narration: The trick: B will simulate A's EAV challenger itself. B sits between a PRG challenger and A, forwarding the PRG challenge string $y$ as if it were the keystream.
If $y = G(s)$, A sees a real encryption and should win with advantage $\varepsilon$. If $y$ is random, A sees a one-time pad and can't win at all. B's decision then reveals which world it is in.
B is the outer box; A lives inside it. Watch B appear and swallow A.

entities.label: Distinguisher B
entities.caption: constructs & runs A as a subroutine

steps.diagramNote: B is the outer box; A is nested inside. B replaces A's challenger.

steps.title: 6 · The PRG Security Game (B's Target)
steps.claim: B must distinguish $G(s)$ from a truly random string $r$.
narration: B plays the PRG indistinguishability game. The PRG challenger flips a bit: in the real world it sends $y = G(s)$ for random $s$; in the random world it sends $y = r \xleftarrow{\$} \{0,1\}^{\ell(n)}$.
B must output $1$ (real) or $0$ (random). Breaking $G$ means guessing correctly with non-negligible advantage. Our job: show B inherits A's advantage $\varepsilon$.
steps.diagramNote: B receives y from the PRG challenger and must decide: real or random?

steps.title: 7 · Construct B: y Becomes the Keystream
steps.claim: B sets $c = y \oplus m_b$ and hands $c$ to A, simulating the EAV challenger.
narration: B receives $y$ and runs A exactly once. B impersonates the EAV challenger:
A submits $m_0, m_1$. B picks a random bit $b$, computes $c = y \oplus m_b$, and returns $c$ to A. A outputs $b'$.
Crucially, B uses the PRG challenge $y$ in place of the keystream $G(k)$. Whether $y$ is real or random completely determines what A sees.
steps.diagramNote: B forwards y as the keystream and plays A's encryption challenger.

steps.title: 8 · Map A's Guess to a Distinguisher Output
steps.claim: B outputs $1$ iff $b' = b$: A wins $\Rightarrow$ B votes "real".
narration: A returns its guess $b'$. B now outputs its own decision to the PRG challenger:
B outputs $1$ (real) when $b' = b$, and $0$ (random) otherwise.
The logic: if A correctly identified the message, the keystream must have been structured (pseudorandom) — so B votes "real". If A failed, the keystream looked random — so B votes "random".
steps.diagramNote: A's correct guess ⇒ B votes 'real'. A's failure ⇒ B votes 'random'.

steps.title: 9 · The Two Worlds
narration: Real world ($y = G(s)$): A's view is exactly the EAV experiment on $\Pi$ — $c = G(s) \oplus m_b$ with $s$ random is distributed as $\mathsf{Enc}_k(m_b)$. So $\Pr[B=1 \mid \text{real}] = \Pr[A \text{ wins}] = \tfrac{1}{2} + \varepsilon$.
Random world ($y = r$): $c = r \oplus m_b$ is a one-time pad with a truly random pad — $c$ is uniform, independent of $b$. A has zero information, so $\Pr[B=1 \mid \text{random}] = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

Therefore $$\begin{aligned}\mathsf{Adv}_B &= \Pr[B=1 \mid \text{real}] - \Pr[B=1 \mid \text{random}] \\ &= (\tfrac{1}{2} + \varepsilon) - \tfrac{1}{2} = \varepsilon = \mathsf{Adv}_A.\end{aligned}$$ B's advantage equals A's, exactly.
steps.diagramNote: Real world ⇒ A wins (adv ε). Random world ⇒ A can't (1/2). Gap = ε = Adv_B.

steps.title: 10 · Contradiction & Conclusion
steps.claim: A non-negligible $\mathsf{Adv}_A$ gives a non-negligible $\mathsf{Adv}_B$ — contradicting PRG security.
narration: If A broke the stream cipher with non-negligible advantage $\varepsilon$, then B breaks the PRG with the same non-negligible advantage $\varepsilon$.
But $G$ is a secure PRG — no efficient distinguisher has non-negligible advantage. Contradiction.
Therefore no such A exists: the stream cipher $\Pi$ is EAV-secure. QED.
steps.diagramNote: Secure G ⇒ no efficient A breaks Π. The reduction preserves advantage exactly.

sequence-of-games.title: Sequential Stream Cipher Security by a Sequence of Games
sequence-of-games.subtitle: A hybrid argument: walking from the real keystream to a one-time pad, one PRG call at a time.
sequence-of-games.theorem: Let $G : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^{2n}$ be a secure PRG. The sequential (stateful) stream cipher iterates $(s_i, y_i) = G(s_{i-1})$ from a seed $s_0 = k$, using block $y_i$ to encrypt the $i$-th message. Over $t$ blocks the keystream is indistinguishable from $t \cdot n$ uniform bits, and the eavesdropping advantage satisfies $\mathsf{Adv}_{\mathrm{cipher}} \le t \cdot \mathsf{Adv}_{\mathrm{prg}}$ — negligible whenever $t = \mathrm{poly}(n)$.

steps.title: 1 · The Sequential Stream Cipher
steps.claim: One seed drives a chain of $G$'s; each step emits a keystream block and a new state.
narration: A sequential (stateful, synchronous) stream cipher stretches one short seed into an unbounded keystream, one block at a time.
Take a length-doubling PRG $G : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^{2n}$ and split its output $G(s) = (s', y)$ into a fresh $n$-bit state $s'$ and an $n$-bit output block $y$.
Starting from the key $s_0 = k$, iterate $(s_i, y_i) = G(s_{i-1})$: emit block $y_i$, keep state $s_i$. The keystream $y_1 \Vert y_2 \Vert \cdots \Vert y_t$ encrypts a stream of messages by XOR.
steps.diagramNote: One seed → a chain of G's. Each G emits a block yᵢ (up) and the next state sᵢ (right).

steps.title: 2 · The Goal, and Why a Sequence of Games
steps.claim: Security $\Leftrightarrow$ real keystream $\approx$ random keystream. We bridge the gap one PRG call at a time.
narration: Encrypting $t$ messages this way is secure iff the keystream $y_1 \ldots y_t$ is indistinguishable from $t \cdot n$ truly random bits. The whole question reduces to the pseudorandomness of the chained output.
So we compare two worlds: the real keystream (from the chain) and the ideal keystream (uniform — a genuine one-time pad). If no efficient distinguisher separates them, the cipher is secure.
But the two worlds differ in all $t$ blocks at once — hard to attack head-on. The sequence-of-games technique interpolates between them with tiny, single-change hops.
steps.diagramNote: Real vs ideal keystream — they differ in all t blocks at once. So we interpolate.

steps.title: 3 · The Sequence of Games
steps.claim: $G_0 =$ real, $G_t =$ ideal; neighbors differ by one block. Bound each rung, then telescope.
narration: Define a chain of hybrid games $G_0, G_1, \ldots, G_t$. In game $G_j$ the first $j$ blocks are truly random and the remaining $t - j$ come from the chain, re-seeded at a fresh random state.
$G_0$ is the real world (nothing random yet — every block from $G$). $G_t$ is the ideal world (every block random). Consecutive games differ in exactly one block.
A distinguisher's advantage is the endpoint gap $\bigl|\Pr[D \to 1 \mid G_0] - \Pr[D \to 1 \mid G_t]\bigr|$. We bound each single-step gap and add them up.
steps.diagramNote: Games G₀ … Gₜ. Neighbors differ in one block; bound each rung of the ladder.

steps.title: 4 · Game G₀ — the Real Keystream
steps.claim: $G_0$ is the real keystream: all $t$ blocks are produced by $G$.
narration: In $G_0$ every block is produced by the chain: $y_i$ is the output half of $G(s_{i-1})$, seeded by the real key $s_0 = k$.
$G_0$ is exactly the experiment a real eavesdropper faces. $\Pr[D \to 1 \mid G_0]$ is the probability our distinguisher outputs $1$ against the true cipher.
steps.diagramNote: G₀: every block comes from the chain (slate = pseudorandom). This is the real cipher.

steps.title: 5 · Anatomy of a Hybrid Game Gᵢ
steps.claim: $G_i$: blocks $1..i$ random; a fresh random state re-seeds the pseudorandom tail $i{+}1..t$.
narration: Game $G_i$ cuts the chain at position $i$: blocks $y_1, \ldots, y_i$ are replaced by truly random strings, and a fresh random state $\hat s_i \xleftarrow{\$} \{0,1\}^n$ re-seeds the chain for blocks $y_{i+1}, \ldots, y_t$.
$G_i$ interpolates: the left part is ideal (random), the right part is real (pseudorandom). $G_0$ has the cut at the far left (nothing random); $G_t$ at the far right (all random).
steps.diagramNote: Gᵢ: blocks 1..i random (green); fresh random state ŝᵢ re-seeds the pseudorandom tail.

steps.title: 6 · One Hop: Gᵢ₋₁ → Gᵢ
steps.claim: Neighbors differ only in whether one pair $(s_i, y_i)$ is $G(\text{uniform})$ or uniform — a single PRG instance.
narration: Fix a neighbor pair. Everything before block $i$ is identical (random), and everything after is the identical chain — given the state $s_i$.

The sole difference: in $G_{i-1}$ the pair $(s_i, y_i)$ is $G(\hat s_{i-1})$ for a uniform $\hat s_{i-1}$; in $G_i$ that same pair is drawn uniformly. One application of $G$, on a uniform input, is all that changes.
That is exactly a PRG challenge: is $(s_i, y_i)$ pseudorandom or uniform? A distinguisher for $G_{i-1}$ vs $G_i$ is a distinguisher for $G$.
steps.diagramNote: The lone change: (sᵢ,yᵢ) = G(random)  vs  uniform — exactly one PRG challenge.

steps.title: 7 · The Reduction Bᵢ Bounds the Hop
steps.claim: $B_i$ plants its PRG challenge at position $i$: real $w \Rightarrow G_{i-1}$, uniform $w \Rightarrow G_i$. Each rung $\le \mathsf{Adv}_{\mathrm{prg}}$.
narration: Distinguisher $B_i$ takes a PRG challenge $w = (s^*, y^*)$ — either $G(s)$ for uniform $s$, or uniform — and builds a full keystream:

blocks $1..i{-}1$ chosen uniformly at random, block $i$ set to $y^*$, and blocks $i{+}1..t$ produced by continuing the chain from state $s^*$. It runs the keystream distinguisher $D$ on this and echoes $D$'s bit.
If $w = G(s)$, then $B_i$ perfectly simulates $G_{i-1}$; if $w$ is uniform, it simulates $G_i$. Hence $\bigl|\Pr[D \to 1 \mid G_{i-1}] - \Pr[D \to 1 \mid G_i]\bigr| \le \mathsf{Adv}_{\mathrm{prg}}$.
steps.diagramNote: Bᵢ plants w at block i: w real ⇒ view = Gᵢ₋₁; w uniform ⇒ view = Gᵢ. Gap ≤ Adv_prg.

steps.title: 8 · Telescoping the Ladder
steps.claim: Triangle inequality over $t$ rungs: total distinguishing advantage $\le t \cdot \mathsf{Adv}_{\mathrm{prg}}$.
narration: Each of the $t$ neighboring gaps is at most $\mathsf{Adv}_{\mathrm{prg}}$. By the triangle inequality the endpoints' gap telescopes:
$$\bigl|\Pr[D{\to}1 \mid G_0] - \Pr[D{\to}1 \mid G_t]\bigr| \;\le\; \sum_{i=1}^{t} \mathsf{Adv}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{prg}} \;\le\; t \cdot \mathsf{Adv}_{\mathrm{prg}}.$$

The $t$ reductions differ only in where they plant the challenge; a single $B$ that first picks $i \xleftarrow{\$} \{1, \ldots, t\}$ attains $\tfrac{1}{t}$ of the sum, giving the clean bound $\mathsf{Adv}_{\mathrm{cipher}} \le t \cdot \mathsf{Adv}_{\mathrm{prg}}$.
steps.diagramNote: Triangle inequality: gap(G₀, Gₜ) ≤ Σ rungs ≤ t · Adv_prg.

steps.title: 9 · Ideal Endpoint & Conclusion
steps.claim: $G_t$ = one-time pad (advantage $0$); poly $\times$ negligible $=$ negligible $\Rightarrow$ the cipher is secure. QED.
narration: At $G_t$ the keystream is $t \cdot n$ uniform bits: a genuine one-time pad. By perfect secrecy the eavesdropper learns nothing — advantage exactly $0$.

Therefore the distinguishing advantage against the real cipher is at most $t \cdot \mathsf{Adv}_{\mathrm{prg}}$. With $t = \mathrm{poly}(n)$ and $\mathsf{Adv}_{\mathrm{prg}}$ negligible, the product is negligible.
The sequential stream cipher inherits the PRG's security, degraded only by the number of blocks $t$. QED.
steps.diagramNote: Gₜ = true one-time pad (advantage 0). poly · negl = negl ⇒ the cipher is secure. QED.
